draft.title: Acquired brain injury
card: An acquired brain injury (ABI) is damage to the brain that happens after birth. It is not present from birth and it is not caused by a condition the person was born with.
Causes include a blow to the head, a stroke (when blood supply to part of the brain is cut off or a vessel bleeds) and a lack of oxygen, such as after near drowning.
Effects depend on which part of the brain is damaged and how badly. Two people with an ABI can be affected in different ways.
An ABI can change biological functioning (such as movement or fatigue), psychological functioning (such as memory, attention or mood) and social functioning (such as relationships, work or study).
draft.remember: An ABI is brain damage after birth, and it can affect body, mind and social life.

a.q: Which of these is an example of an acquired brain injury?
opts: Damage from a stroke at age 60
Brain damage from a genetic condition present at birth
Normal loss of some brain cells during sleep
A change in mood caused by a bad day at school
a.why: A stroke damages the brain after birth, so it is an ABI. A condition present from birth is not acquired. A bad mood or sleep does not involve damage to the brain.
a.clue: Look for damage that happens after birth.

b.q: Jaxon fell from his bike and hit his head. Months later he forgets recent conversations and no longer meets his friends. Which statement best describes his situation?
opts: The ABI has affected psychological and social functioning
The ABI has affected only his biological functioning
The effects show that the injury was present from birth
Any person with an ABI would have the same effects as Jaxon
b.why: Forgetting conversations is a psychological change, and no longer meeting friends is a social change. The effects of an ABI depend on which part of the brain is damaged and how badly, so they differ between people.
b.clue: Sort memory and friendships into the three types of functioning.

a.best: Damage from a stroke at age 60

b.best: The ABI has affected psychological and social functioning
